extracted.intended_audience: Bellingcat Justice & Accountability Unit investigators / open-source investigators working on Ukraine
extracted.subtask_description: Methodology and operational guidance for Bellingcat/GLAN investigators conducting online open source investigations (OOSI) into incidents in Ukraine, with special annexes on sexual & gender-based violence (SGBV), crimes affecting children (CAAC), and legal evidence handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) and sexual crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual violence includes acts such as sexual slavery, forced prostitution, forced pregnancy, forced nudity, trafficking, forced abortion or sterilization, and sexual torture. Sexual crimes are “physical and non-physcial acts with a sexual element” which constitute crimes as defined broadly by international laws or progressive national legal systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites International Protocol and ICC policy papers. Use these definitions when identifying and classifying content; sexual crimes may be physical or non-physical and may be criminalised under international law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Gender-based crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender-based crimes are those committed against persons, whether male or female, because of their sex and/or socially constructed gender roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are not always sexual in nature and may include non-sexual attacks on people because of their gender; consider gender persecution under Rome Statute Article 7(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender perspective requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A gender perspective requires an understanding of differences in status, power, roles, and needs between males and females, and the impact of gender on people’s opportunities and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should integrate this perspective to avoid reinforcing gender norms or biases and to better understand how gender impacted crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender analysis as an investigative tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender analysis is a tool to examine, analyse, and understand power dynamics and interactions, inequalities, and differences between different genders and how they impact societal norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J&A Unit will conduct a gender analysis for each major investigation and integrate it into investigations as a whole rather than as a separate exercise (see UN OHCHR and academic references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersectional approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account the intersection of discriminatory qualities faced by individuals such as age, race, gender identity, sex, socio-economic status, religion, culture, sexual orientation to contextualise acts and understand how they are sexual in nature and their gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intersectional framing to identify risk and impact on marginalized groups (e.g., LGBTQI persons, persons with disabilities, elderly women, Roma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do no harm principle for SGBV/CAAC
rubrics_metrics.description: The J&A Unit adopts a 'do no harm' approach to all investigations, particularly relating to SGBV and crimes against children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take additional sensitivities and ethical considerations into account, protect dignity of victims, and apply restrictive handling where necessary (see International Protocol and OHCHR guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate investigation plan for SGBV incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: If an incident specifically involving SGBV is selected through triage, create a separate investigation plan including a list of search terms that may be used colloquially to refer to SGBV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor search strategy and documentation to SGBV context and include colloquial/vernacular terms that may indicate SGBV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure storage and access restriction for sensitive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific content relating to SGBV and crimes against children will be held in a highly secure manner to protect identities of victims and alleged perpetrators; viewing of dignity-eroding content will be restricted on a need-to-access basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize Uwazi database so such content can be filtered out where necessary; investigators must not publicly post/repost this content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent and sharing policy for SGBV material
rubrics_metrics.description: In OOSI it will often be impossible to obtain informed consent from victims; therefore, the J&A Unit will only share SGBV information with prosecutorial/international bodies or partners after considering relevant policies they have in place to protect sanctity and dignity of victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sharing, check partner policies and restrict disclosures appropriately to minimise harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tagging policy: 'Possible SGBV' for direct visual evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any photograph or video depicting possible direct evidence of SGBV (Direct SGBV) will be tagged as 'possible SGBV' in Uwazi and additional tagging systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables easy identification and transfer of such incidents to international/prosecutorial bodies even if little other information is available; examples include a video of rape or a photograph of a nude prisoner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Hague Principles indicia to identify sexual acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague Principles set out indicia that can define content as sexual in nature, including: exposure or contact with sexual body parts; intent or perception of sexual nature; perpetrator or third party deriving sexual gratification; impact on sexual autonomy/integrity/reproductive capacity; sexual innuendo/sexualised language; use/control/degradation of fluids or tissue associated with sexual/reproductive capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these indicia when determining whether an act is sexual in nature, including in cases without physical contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and scope of direct SGBV
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include rape (Rome Statute definition), other acts of a sexual nature (physical or interpretable as sexual), nudity/partial nudity (victims, perpetrators, third parties), and non-physical sexual violence (e.g., perpetrators joking about sexual violence in front of detainees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember sexual violence can occur without physical contact; also note that gender-based violence can be non-sexual (e.g., killing because of gender). Cross-reference Rome Statute crimes (rape, sexual slavery, forced pregnancy, enforced sterilization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tagging policy: 'SGBV Red Flag' for indicia/indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that exhibits indications or 'red flags' for SGBV but does not contain direct SGBV will be tagged with 'SGBV Red Flag' in Uwazi and any additional tagging systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should provide a text box explanation for why they selected Possible SGBV or SGBV Red Flag. The tag helps flag leads for prosecutorial bodies even when direct evidence is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags — Attacks & Occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential indicators under Attacks & Occupation: takeover/occupation of homes/villages; checkpoints in/near hospitals, schools, religious centres; targeting specific groups (men of fighting age, women/girls, children, LGBTQI+); distinct treatment of men vs women; elderly people (especially women) living alone; reports/indications groups of women/girls held in private locations; verbal/written sexual threats/harassment; humiliating treatment; bodies found dead alone or in small groups (indicative of rape prior to death); burnt bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These situational indicators may suggest SGBV even if not directly depicted; use them to justify SGBV Red Flag tagging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags — Arrests & Detentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators include mass detentions of one sex/gender/age; strip or body searches; humiliating treatment; interrogation/torture while detained; targeting of women/girls or men/boys separately for arrests; housing male and female prisoners together; detaining women/girls under male rather than female guards; injuries related to sexual or reproductive organs; reports/images of any form of nudity during arrest/detention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signs during detention contexts can be indicia of SGBV and should be flagged accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags — Recruitment & Training
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators include recruitment targeted at women/girls by parties to the conflict; forced conscription of men/boys in occupied areas; forced performance of sexual acts/forced nudity as part of training; civilian women and children present in military camps or barracks; social media showing members of armed forces condoning or joking about SGBV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for training/recruitment-related behaviours and online content that normalises or demonstrates SGBV-related practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags — Campaigns and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports by people on the ground, civil society organisations, or media of SGBV; advocacy or social media campaigns against SGBV; statements by parties condemning SGBV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such reporting/campaign activity can corroborate or indicate the presence of SGBV and should inform tagging and further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags — Humanitarian situation risk indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanitarian risk factors increasing SGBV risk include lack of internet/mobile connection; poor security/infrastructure; presence of vulnerable populations; discrimination when seeking shelter (including trans persons, elderly, disabled, LGBTQI+); informal/unvetted shelters; increased numbers of displaced women/girls/children or travelling alone; reports from healthcare providers (e.g., increased sexual health inquiries); discrimination or reports of discrimination against women and girls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these contextual risk factors when assessing SGBV likelihood; they are overarching rather than discrete red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and tagging: Crimes Against and Affecting Children (CAAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAAC concerns crimes committed against all people below age 18. Any photograph or video depicting possible direct evidence of crimes against children (obviously a child) will be tagged as 'children visible' and pieces with indications/red flags will be tagged 'CAAC Red Flag'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should take a restrictive approach and only tag CAAC Red Flag if not already covered by another tag to avoid over-tagging. Use similar protective storage/handling as for SGBV content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Grave Violations Against Children (identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: United Nations' Six Grave Violations: (a) recruitment and use of children; (b) killing or maiming of children; (c) sexual violence against children; (d) attacks against schools or hospitals; (e) abduction of children; (f) denial of humanitarian access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to identify and classify harms affecting children in armed conflict settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: CAAC Red Flags — contextual categories
rubrics_metrics.description: CAAC Red Flags categories include Attacks & Occupation (presence of children in conflict/occupied areas; targeting schools/playgrounds; presence of children when family members are attacked; transport of groups of children; children born during occupation/rape), Detention (detention/interrogation/torture of children), Recruitment & Training (use of child soldiers, recruitment aimed at young audiences, forced conscription under 18, children in military camps), Campaigns Against CAAC (reports, advocacy, statements), and Humanitarian indicators (increased children travelling alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of overlap with SGBV tags, brief investigators to avoid duplicate tagging; include text-box explanations when tagging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal: investigators must be prepared to testify and accept legal scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in J&A Unit assumes willingness to appear as a witness; investigators may be asked in court about how material was obtained, processed and stored and will face cross-examination on credibility, memory, motives, and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain rigorous documentation and be prepared to explain methodology to withstand legal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence considerations: relevance, admissibility, authenticity, reliability, and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence relevance (probative/disprobative) is the first test; admissibility may be impacted by exclusionary rules (e.g., unfairness). Authenticity (not doctored) and reliability (content is reliable and testable) are central. ICC places more emphasis on weight than admissibility; methodical verification work increases probative weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design investigations and verification to maximise authenticity and reliability; anticipate different jurisdictional standards (e.g., England & Wales vs ICC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearsay caution and verification value
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearsay is generally inadmissible in some jurisdictions (England & Wales) and treated with caution at the ICC; OOSI content often contains or is accompanied by hearsay statements which should be verified where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect supporting verification and provenance information; a video may be used as evidence of what it shows but not necessarily as proof of an accompanying statement without further verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: pursue all lines of reasonable enquiry including exculpatory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators must search for information that could explain an attack or suggest alternative attribution, including evidence that could exonerate a suspect or suggest non-criminal explanations (e.g., presence of military targets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document lines of enquiry and include exculpatory searches in the Table of Factual Inquiries to demonstrate impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record searches and maintain search logs (use of Hunchly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a log of search terms in addition to using Hunchly, which tracks online activity, to demonstrate how content was found and that searches were unbiased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The log helps show investigators pursued all reasonable lines of inquiry; include search terms, timestamps and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardise search starting conditions (use of VPNs and clearing cookies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use VPNs and clear cookies before creating new research accounts to create a standardised starting point in respect of information available to search algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures are taken out of caution to reduce algorithmic personalization effects; document these steps in methodology logs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain all relevant content and background material for potential disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain relevant background information that could undermine the prosecution case or assist the defence (e.g., anything bearing on witness reliability, motives to fabricate, admissibility issues, alternative suspect information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include rough drafts of victim statements, notes, metadata, or material pointing to another person’s involvement. Retention supports disclosure obligations and credibility under cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility fairness/exclusion balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may exclude otherwise relevant evidence if admitting it would have an unacceptably adverse effect on the fairness of proceedings; judges balance probative value against prejudicial effect (applies in England & Wales and similarly at ICC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification and methodological rigour can reduce exclusion risk by increasing probative value and reducing unfair prejudice.
